comment: Brian (ElevenLabs) VO for the 5-minute PLAYER DRAMA FILM 'Lukaku — The Promise' (300s). A drama-mystery: an idol's secret revealed. ALL facts VERIFIED (sources in README.md): Romelu Lukaku, b. 13 May 1993 Antwerp; aged ~6 saw his mother mix WATER into the milk to make it last ('we were broke, not just poor'); father Roger Lukaku an ex-pro footballer whose career/income ended; social housing, up to ~3 weeks with no electricity, mattress on floor, bread+milk lunches; grandfather's dying wish to take care of his mother; vowed to be pro by 16 and made his Anderlecht debut at exactly 16 (2009); clubs incl. Everton, Man Utd (42 goals), Inter Milan (64 goals, 2020-21 Serie A title), Chelsea, Roma; BELGIUM ALL-TIME TOP SCORER (89 goals, 124 caps by Nov 2025); 300+ career goals; played WCs 2014/2018/2022 & Euros 2016/2020/2024; publicly described racist double-standard ('Belgian striker' when scoring vs 'Belgian striker of Congolese descent' when not). SOCCER ONLY — round-neck shirts, a pitch with goals, NO helmets/pads. NO on-screen subtitles (CLAUDE.md #10): Brian's voice carries it; only minimal furniture (name/year labels, the worldcup26.world CTA). Numbers spelled as words for clean TTS; keep lines short.

lines.text: Last night, a stadium shook. One man rose highest — and the net snapped tight.
The cameras found an idol. The world saw a giant. Almost nobody saw the secret he still carries.
This is the story of Romelu Lukaku — and a promise no one was ever supposed to know.
Antwerp, Belgium. A boy, six years old, opens the refrigerator before school.
He watches his mother pour water into the last of the milk — to stretch it one more day.
That was the morning he understood. They were not just poor. They were broke.
His father, Roger, had been a footballer too — until it ended, and the money ran out.
Social housing. Some weeks, no electricity for twenty days. A mattress on the floor. Bread and milk.
And a grandfather's last words to a frightened child: take care of your mother.
So the boy made a promise — silent, stubborn, impossible.
He would be a professional footballer by the age of sixteen. He would buy back her smile.
He stopped playing like a child. He played like a son with a debt to repay.
Rupel Boom at six. Lierse at thirteen. Then the academy of Anderlecht.
And on the day it mattered most, he made his professional debut at exactly sixteen years old.
The promise — kept. But this was only the beginning.
England came calling. Chelsea. West Brom. Everton. Then Manchester United — forty-two goals.
Then Italy. Inter Milan. Sixty-four goals — and a league title torn back from the rivals across the city.
And for Belgium's golden generation, he became something no one before him had ever been.
His nation's greatest goalscorer of all time. Eighty-nine goals. The record, his.
Three World Cups. Three European Championships. More than three hundred goals across a career.
The broke boy from Antwerp had become an idol to millions.
But idols are tested. And his hardest opponent never wore a shirt.
He said it himself. When he scored, the headlines called him the Belgian striker.
When he missed, they called him the Belgian striker of Congolese descent.
Same man. Same shirt. He carried that too — and answered the only way he knew. Goals.
Because every goal was never really for the crowd.
It was for a woman at a refrigerator, on a cold Antwerp morning, making the milk last one more day.
Football did not only make Romelu Lukaku rich. It let him keep his word.
And that is what turns a player into an idol — not the trophies, but the debt he refused to forget.
So when you see him roar after a goal — now you know the secret.
He is still that six-year-old boy. And he is still keeping his promise.
